title: Prince Robinson, the underrated tenor player
summary: Tate admires Prince Robinson of McKinney's Cotton Pickers and explains why he never got his due.

story.theme_name: The reed and horn player's craft: clarinet, sax, tone
story.community_name: Coleman Hawkins and the great saxophonists

blocks.x: And then all the time though, after Milton, I was listening to a tenor player, me and Herschel, also Milton, by the name of Prince Robinson. That's Harold Vick's uncle.
Uh-huh. And he played with McKinney's Cotton Pickers. I love the way he played. He never got the recognition that was due him.
Roy Eldridge once told me that when he was coming up, the two great players were Hawkins and Prince.

That's right, that's right. Prince didn't get the recognition he deserved, he never did. He played, man, he did some -- he really swung and knew his instrument very well. He played some things that were very exciting and we used to listen to him quite a bit because actually, Prince

was smoother than Hawk at that time. He didn't have as big a sound as Hawk, but he was a little smoother than Hawk in his executions and things like that and we used to listen to him. He got over that horn. He played like, you know, and was really making it, you know. And we listened to him until Hawk -- Fletcher made "Stampede" and Hawk made "Stampede" and we forgot about everybody in the world.
He wiped out everybody in the world then after he played "Stampede." We all said, no, here's where it's at, with that big sound and everything.
What happened to Prince? Why didn't he (inaudible)?

I don't know. Sometimes it happens because -- and it was like -- now Jean Goldkette, they worked at the Greystone Ballroom and Jean Goldkette managed them, too. So they were the black band that played and whenever Jean Goldkette went out, they went out. So there was no need. I don't know why he didn't get the recognition because he was on the scene and there were people coming out of Fletcher's band like they used to go out of Whiteman's to Goldkette. They used to do that, you know. And they were doing that with Fletcher and McKinney's Cotton Pickers, same thing, and Don Redman would work with Fletcher a while and then he'd go work McKinney's Cotton Pickers, he and Benny Carter and all of them.

But he just never -- he never captured the recognition that he should have gotten and of course, you know, like in the years he started declining, styles and things change, you know, people forgot all about him. But Hawk liked him, too. He said a lot of nice things about -- I mean, even to me.

Well, Prince is from Norfolk, Virginia and he and Ed Cuffee and all were both with the McKinney's Cotton Pickers and of course, he died here in New York, you know. He moved here to New York after joining McKinney's Cotton Pickers. He came on here to New York. He worked around here in New York. But he -- I guess after Hawk gained such a big reputation, you know, after "Stampede," everybody was scared to even pick up a horn around Hawk.
